region.text: Parthia and Hyrcania in Cliopatria's outline, the satrapy of Andragoras

ledger.note: 238 BC: Arsaces I and his brother Tiridates I seize Parthia from Andragoras. 'about 238 BC' the Parni, under Arsaces and his brother Tiridates I, invaded Parthia and seized Astabene from Andragoras; 'A short while later, the Parni seized the rest of Parthia from Andragoras, killing him'; Hyrcania 'was shortly conquered by the Parni as well' (undated). The infobox counts the era from 247 BC (Arsaces crowned at Asaak, 'probably in c. 247 BC'); Curtis and Brosius put Andragoras's overthrow at 238 (Parthian Empire page). Cliopatria starts its shape in -239.

209 BC: Parthia submits to Antiochus III (bridged). The Arsaces I page does not mention Antiochus III's campaign or a vassalage; the dates are those of the seleucid-empire dossier (vassal 209-188, from its Seleucid Empire and Roman-Seleucid war pages). Parthia is the vassal here; the tint is drawn from the Seleucid ledger.

region.text: Margiana and Aria, the domains of Eucratides taken in 163-155

region.text: Aria and Margiana; 'Merv became a stronghold of Parthian dominance in the northeast'

ledger.note: 158 BC: Mithridates I takes Aria and Margiana. He defeated Eucratides and took Aria, Margiana and western Bactria between 163 and 155; 158 is the Greco-Bactrian dossier's date inside that span; 'Eucratides was supposedly made a Parthian vassal'.
158 BC: the fighting with Eucratides ends with Aria and Margiana Parthian (year bridged inside the page's 163-155 span).

147 BC: Atropatene is subdued (the second year of the page's '148/7 BC').

The Mithridates I page gives the conquest ('conquering Media and Atropatene in 148/7 BC'; 'This victory was followed by the Parthian conquest of Media Atropatene') but not the status: 'The page does not say whether Atropatene ... became a vassal'. region.text: Babylonia and Seleucia on the Tigris

region.text: Susiana with Susa, the kingdom of Elymais

138 BC: Demetrius II 'was defeated and captured in 138 BC'; the Parthian Empire page says 140 BC for the invasion and its defeat.

Kings of Persis page: 'Later the frataraka Wadfradad II (fl. 138 BC) was made a vassal of the Iranian Parthian (Arsacid) Empire'; 'The Parthian Empire then took control of Persis under Arsacid king Mithridates I (ca. 171-138 BC)'; Strabo, quoted there: the early kings were Seleucid tributaries 'until c.140 BC, when the Parthians conquered the region'. 130 BC: Babylonia and Susa are lost to the Seleucid king Antiochus VII (130-129 BC on the page).

region.text: Assyria and lower Mesopotamia with Ctesiphon and Adiabene

ledger.note: 116 AD: Trajan takes Seleucia and Ctesiphon. He 'dragged his fleet overland into the Tigris and captured Seleucia and finally the Parthian capital of Ctesiphon', then received 'the submission of Athambelus, the ruler of Charax' (the introduction dates Ctesiphon 115; the roman-empire dossier dates it 115).

He 'installed a Parthian prince, Parthamaspates, as a client ruler and withdrew to Syria' and died in 117; Rome 'relinquished Armenia, Mesopotamia, and Assyria' and 'the Euphrates once again became the frontier'. 117 AD: northern Mesopotamia returns to Parthia. Hadrian returned Armenia, Mesopotamia and Adiabene to their previous rulers and client kings (undated beyond 117-138).

161 AD: Armenia under Vologases's king. 'Vologases entered the Kingdom of Armenia, expelled its king and installed his own.'

163 AD: Statius Priscus takes Artaxata. His legions achieved success 'during the campaign season of 163, culminating with the capture of the Armenian capital Artaxata'; Sohaemus was hailed on coinage of 164 as 'Rex armeniis Datus'.

165 AD: Rome keeps its gains in upper Mesopotamia. 'Edessa was re-occupied, Mannus re-installed'; the infobox: 'Minor Roman gains in upper Mesopotamia'; 'Nisibis ... remained in Roman hands for several decades'.

region.text: upper and lower Mesopotamia, the ground of Cassius's campaign

195 AD: Severus invades Mesopotamia and occupies Seleucia and Babylon.

region.text: northern Mesopotamia as far as Nisibis and Singara

197 AD: Severus withdraws from Ctesiphon with northern Mesopotamia annexed.

wars.name: Seleucid expedition of Seleucus II against Arsaces I
wars.outcome: The Seleucids recovered Parthia briefly: Arsaces made peace with the Greco-Bactrian ruler Diodotus II, withdrew to the Apasiacae, and later regained his territories.
wars.note: 'A recovery expedition by the Seleucids under Seleucus II was made in 228 BC'; the Seleucid conquest was short-lived. The page dates neither the loss nor the recovery, so there are no contest events.

wars.name: Mithridates I's war with Eucratides of Bactria
wars.outcome: Parthian victory: Aria, Margiana and western Bactria taken; Eucratides 'supposedly made a Parthian vassal'.

wars.name: Mithridates I's conquest of Media and Mesopotamia
wars.outcome: Media and Atropatene fell in 148/147, Babylonia in 141; Demetrius II was captured in 138.

wars.name: Antiochus VII's eastern campaign
wars.outcome: Antiochus VII retook Babylonia and Susa, then was killed at Ecbatana in 129 BC; the Seleucids lost the east for good.

wars.name: Parthian-Saka wars
wars.outcome: The Saka killed Phraates II (c. 127) and the nomads killed Artabanus I (c. 124); Mithridates II retook Sakastan between 124 and 115 and gave it to the House of Suren.
wars.note: Mithridates II page: 'He sent a Suren-led army to retake Sakastan' (124-115).

wars.name: Mithridates II's Armenian and Mesopotamian campaigns
wars.outcome: Armenia accepted Parthian suzerainty (c. 120); Adiabene, Gordyene and Osroene acknowledged Parthian authority by 95 and the western border reached the Euphrates.
wars.note: The Mithridates II page also has Sulla meet Orobazus in 96 BC; the Parthian Empire page reads that meeting as a Euphrates border agreement (c. 96/95) and says historians dispute Sulla's authority; the Roman-Parthian Wars page dates the talks c. 105 and does not mention the Euphrates. No contest event.

wars.name: Tigranes the Great's reconquest
wars.outcome: Armenia 'retook Adiabene, Gordyene, and Media Atropatene' and the seventy valleys while Parthia was in its Dark Age after Mithridates II.

wars.name: Parthian attack on Gordyene and Pompey's arbitration
wars.outcome: Parthia took Mesopotamia except the western district of Osroene; Pompey arbitrated over Corduene; Phraates abandoned the siege of Artaxata.

wars.name: Crassus's Parthian campaign
wars.outcome: Parthian victory at Carrhae (53 BC): Crassus and his son killed, the eagles taken; no border change.

wars.name: Parthian invasion of Syria (51 BC)
wars.outcome: Pacorus and Osaces besieged Cassius in Antioch; Cassius ambushed them near Antigoneia and Osaces was killed; no border change.

wars.name: Parthian invasion of Syria and Judea
wars.outcome: Pacorus and Labienus held Syria and installed Antigonus in Judea; Ventidius won at the Cilician Gates (39) and Mount Gindarus (38, Pacorus killed); Herod ousted Antigonus in 37.

wars.name: Antony's Parthian War
wars.outcome: Antony's invasion of Media Atropatene failed after Phraates IV ambushed his rear detachment; no border change.

wars.name: Roman-Parthian war over Armenia
wars.outcome: Peace of Rhandeia (63): Tiridates and his descendants rule Armenia on condition that they receive the kingship from the Roman emperor.

wars.name: Trajan's Parthian campaign
wars.outcome: Trajan annexed Armenia (114) and northern Mesopotamia (115), took Seleucia and Ctesiphon (116) and reached Charax; revolts and the failed siege of Hatra forced a retreat; Hadrian gave up the conquests.

wars.name: Roman-Parthian War of 161-166
wars.outcome: Roman victory: Armenia 'reconstructed on Roman terms', Ctesiphon taken and burned in 165, 'Minor Roman gains in upper Mesopotamia'.

wars.name: Severus's Parthian war
wars.outcome: Severus occupied Seleucia and Babylon (195), sacked Ctesiphon (197) and failed at Hatra; Rome kept northern Mesopotamia as far as Nisibis and Singara.

wars.name: Caracalla's and Macrinus's Parthian war
wars.outcome: Caracalla sacked Arbela (216); Macrinus lost the battle of Nisibis (217) and paid Parthia over 200 million denarii; no border change.

wars.name: Ardashir's revolt and the Battle of Hormozdgan

zones.text: Persis, Kerman, Isfahan, Susiana and the Gulf coast

wars.outcome: Ardashir took Persis (211/2), then Kerman, Isfahan, Susa and Characene, and defeated and killed Artabanus IV at Hormozdgan on 28 April 224; the Parthian dynasty ended.
wars.note: Papak's takeover of Istakhr 'between the years 205 and 206' is the page's earliest date.

certainty.note: No treaty or survey line in these centuries. The Euphrates boundary agreed with Sulla (c. 96/95 BC, disputed on the pages) and the 20 BC exchange of the standards were agreements, not surveyed borders.
The Euphrates frontier with Rome after Hadrian is the page's 'limit of direct Roman control' but moved with every war (115, 117, 165, 197); the Kushan and steppe frontiers are approximate.

notes:
Cliopatria's 28 shapes reviewed against nine pages (the budget for 28 shapes is nine). Founding is 238 BC (Arsaces I page; Curtis and Brosius in the Parthian Empire page), not Cliopatria's -239 and not the 247 BC era of the infobox, which dates Arsaces's coronation. End is 224 (Hormozdgan), not Cliopatria's 237: the 224-237 rump has no page and the Sasanian row takes it at 224. Wrong or adjusted Cliopatria rows: -164..-145 already holds Media, Persis and Sistan (conquered 148-130s); -110..-92 lacks the eastern gains of 124-115; -40..-37 holds Syria two years too long; 114-116 shows no Roman conquest and 117-126 keeps Trajan's Mesopotamia after Hadrian gave it up; 127-153 and 161-164 are padded with Cliopatria's Armenian footprint (Cliopatria has no Armenia 114-153 and 161-164); 184-196 and 207-214 return Roman Mesopotamia to Parthia; 224-237 is a rump. Open gaps: (1) Antiochus III's campaign of 209 and the Seleucid vassalage 209-188 are not on the Arsaces I page; the two events are confidence 1, copied from the seleucid-empire dossier. (2) The Arsaces II and Phriapatius-to-Phraates I reigns (c. 217-165) have no territorial event on the pages; a gap-filler should open 'Arsaces II of Parthia' and 'Phraates I'. (3) Cliopatria drops Margiana from -144 to -92 and the Pakistani cells appear only at -91; no page dates either. (4) The 130s-BC loss of Media to the Seleucid reconquest and Hyrcania's conquest date are undated. (5) Persis's date is the 130s only; Elymais, Characene, Hatra, Persis have no Cliopatria rows and need their own dossiers (me-06-x). Page disagreements: Sulla and the Euphrates (Parthian Empire page c. 96/95 BC border agreement; Roman-Parthian Wars page c. 105 BC talks, Euphrates not mentioned); Ctesiphon under Trajan (115 in the introduction of the Trajan page, 116 in its account); Antiochus VII 133-129 (seleucid-empire dossier) against 130-129 (Parthian Empire page); the Saka gain 126 (indo-scythians) against c. 127; the Sakastan recovery 124-115 (Mithridates II page) against c. 100 (indo-scythians dossier); Nisibis Roman after 166 (161-166 page) against acquired 195-197 (Roman-Parthian Wars page). Names the gazetteer lacks: Characene (head of the Persian Gulf, lower Tigris and Euphrates, capital Charax). Elymais is read as Khuzestan. Counterparts needing dossiers: characene, elymais, persis, kingdom-of-kinda is not used. The rulers key is omitted: the pages give only the first and last Arsacid and a few reign dates (Mithridates I 165-132, Mithridates II 124-91, Vologases I c. 51-77, Vologases IV c. 147-191, Vologases V c. 191-208, Vologases VI c. 208-222, Artabanus IV c. 213-224), not a full list.
